methods.label: Track only the last two digits in each base
methods.explanation:
Only the two rightmost digits affect the condition, so the higher digits can be ignored after the written representations are treated as decimal integers. We use \(X\equiv Y\pmod q\) to mean that \(q\) divides \(X-Y\).

Let the final two base-\(5\) digits be \(u,r\), and the final two base-\(6\) digits be \(v,s\). Thus \(0\le u,r\le4\) and \(0\le v,s\le5\). When read as decimal integers, their sum satisfies
\[
S\equiv10(u+v)+r+s\pmod{100}.
\]
The requested condition is \(S\equiv2N\pmod{100}\).

First reduce this condition modulo \(5\). Since \(N\equiv r\pmod5\), it gives
\[
r+s\equiv2r\pmod5,
\qquad s\equiv r\pmod5.
\]
Within the digit ranges, either \(s=r\), or \((r,s)=(0,5)\). The latter is impossible: \(S\) would be odd, whereas \(2N\) is even. Hence \(r=s\), with \(0\le r\le4\).

Now \(N-r\) is divisible by both \(5\) and \(6\), so write
\[
N=30k+r.
\]
The three-digit restriction is exactly \(4\le k\le33\), with all five choices of \(r\) allowed for each such \(k\).

Removing the final digit and dividing by the base identifies the next digit. In base \(5\), the quotient is \((N-r)/5=6k\), so \(u\) is the remainder of \(k\) upon division by \(5\). In base \(6\), the quotient is \((N-r)/6=5k\), so
\[
u\equiv k\pmod5,
\qquad v\equiv-k\pmod6.
\]
Since the common units digit contributes \(2r\) to both \(S\) and \(2N\), the remaining requirement is
\[
10(u+v)\equiv60k\pmod{100},
\]
or equivalently
\[
u+v\equiv6k\pmod{10}.
\]
Write \(k=5q+u\) for an integer \(q\). Then \(6k\equiv6u\pmod{10}\), so the condition becomes
\[
v\equiv5u\pmod{10}.
\]
Because \(0\le v\le5\), this has just two cases:

If \(u\) is even, then \(v=0\), so \(k\) is divisible by \(6\). In the interval \(4\le k\le33\), these values are \(6,12,18,24,30\). Their remainders modulo \(5\) are \(1,2,3,4,0\), respectively, so the even-remainder choices are \(12,24,30\).

If \(u\) is odd, then \(v=5\), so \(k\equiv1\pmod6\). The possible values are \(7,13,19,25,31\), whose remainders modulo \(5\) are \(2,3,4,0,1\). The odd-remainder choices are \(13,31\).

Thus exactly five values of \(k\) work: \(12,13,24,30,31\). Every one allows all five values \(r=0,1,2,3,4\). The conditions above are equivalent to the required last-two-digit equality, and distinct pairs \((k,r)\) give distinct integers \(N\). Therefore the count is \(5\cdot5=\boxed{25}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).

Basic congruence arithmetic and the common multiple 30 support that work. The method extracts digits through integer quotients and remainders, so a floor-function node is unnecessary. The two final cases are disjoint, exhaustive, and establish sufficiency as well as necessity.

The tens digits satisfy u≡k modulo 5 and v≡-k modulo 6; the required condition is equivalent to v≡5u modulo 10. The exhaustive cases yield k=12,13,24,30,31, each with five distinct valid choices of r, totaling 25.
